profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a SaaS company after the team's internal benchmark for ML-based software defect detection suddenly became unreproducible: the latest rerun shows a 12-point drop in recall for the gradient-boosted defect predictor on the 'Eclipse-3.0' and 'Lucene-2.4' module datasets, while an earlier run from two weeks ago looked strong enough to include in a draft engineering note. The meeting is between the engineer who owns the benchmarking pipeline and the MLOps engineer who maintains experiment infrastructure. Their agenda is to diagnose why the benchmark results shifted, determine whether the issue is with the model, data handling, or execution environment, and agree on a concrete fix path before results are circulated to the wider reliability team. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan, a chosen immediate remediation, and an agreed statement of what it means to have 'fixed' the benchmark instability.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Defect prediction models, experimental design, feature engineering on software metrics datasets, Python model pipelines
members.background: Nina built the comparative benchmark notebook that evaluates random forest, XGBoost, and logistic regression on public software defect datasets adapted into the company's internal evaluation harness.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve confidence in the benchmark because the draft note is already being referenced by engineering leadership, and she worries the problem is a small reproducibility glitch rather than a substantive flaw in the modeling setup.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the benchmark,' they mean the published comparison configuration used in her draft note, which excludes temporary exploratory preprocessing branches.
A run is 'reproducible' if rerunning the official pipeline on the same dataset family yields materially similar aggregate metrics, even if fold-level results differ.
The 'Eclipse-3.0' dataset in the benchmark refers to the cleaned parquet snapshot checked into the feature-store export from last month, not the raw CSV mirrored from PROMISE.
Saying 'same environment' mainly means same package versions and random seeds in the training container, because the hardware and job launcher should not materially affect tabular model outputs.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Experiment tracking, containerized training infrastructure, data lineage, CI/CD for ML workflows
members.background: Marcus recently migrated the benchmark jobs from ad hoc notebook execution to a scheduled runner in the company's ML platform, adding artifact versioning and automatic dataset pulls.
members.private_state: He wants to ensure the platform migration is not blamed unfairly, and he is focused on narrowing the issue to a traceable infrastructure or data-version discrepancy that can be corrected with process controls.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the benchmark,' they mean the currently scheduled pipeline registered in the ML platform, including the default preprocessing module now attached to all tabular jobs.
A run is 'reproducible' only if the same commit and registered assets produce the same per-fold outputs and logged artifacts, not just similar summary metrics.
The 'Eclipse-3.0' dataset refers to the dataset asset ID in the registry, which may transparently point to a refreshed raw-ingest version as long as the schema is unchanged.
Saying 'same environment' includes the full execution context: container image, CPU architecture, library build variants, mounted feature transforms, and orchestrator-injected defaults.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss rerunning 'the benchmark' and comparing it to the earlier result.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the specific comparison setup from her draft note: fixed cleaned snapshots, hand-selected preprocessing, and the notebook-backed evaluation harness used for the earlier headline numbers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the productionized scheduled benchmark job in the ML platform, which includes the platform's default tabular preprocessing stage and current registered assets.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is only one obvious benchmark because the migration from notebook to scheduled runner was framed internally as a straightforward operationalization of the same work, so the phrase feels unambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention anomalies on 'Eclipse-3.0' and 'Lucene-2.4' as if referring to the same datasets.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the cleaned parquet snapshots exported last month after dropping duplicate modules and normalizing missing CK metrics.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the registry assets with those names, which were recently refreshed from raw source files but kept the same human-readable dataset labels.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Dataset names are stable and familiar, so neither expects that the same label could silently point to different physical artifacts with slightly different row counts and imputations.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have 'fixed reproducibility'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree they need to 'get reproducibility back' before sharing results.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means restoring roughly the same aggregate benchmark table, especially comparable recall and AUC ranges, so the report remains trustworthy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means exact or near-exact reproduction of fold-level outputs and tracked artifacts from a pinned run, even if aggregate metrics remain lower than the old report.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML teams, 'reproducibility' is a strongly positive shared term; both think they are endorsing the same goal and do not notice that one is using a report-level standard while the other is using an artifact-level standard.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in checking the 'same environment'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to verify whether the rerun used the 'same environment' as the earlier experiment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to compare Python package versions, model seeds, and key training parameters inside the container.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to compare the entire execution envelope, including image digest, runner type, CPU instruction set, mounted preprocessing plugin, and orchestrator defaults.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds routine and technical enough that each assumes the other naturally includes the same checks they always perform, so the difference in boundaries stays implicit.

turns.inner_thought: The numbers in my draft note came from the published comparison setup in the notebook-backed harness, using the cleaned parquet snapshots from last month. If the latest rerun is suddenly down 12 points on recall for XGBoost on Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4, I really want this to be a narrow reproducibility glitch, not evidence that the benchmark itself was shaky. Leadership has already started citing that table.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to sync quickly because the latest rerun of the benchmark came back with a pretty noticeable recall drop on Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4 versus the numbers in my draft note. The rest of the table is not wildly off, but those two are far enough down that I don't want us circulating anything until we understand it.

turns.inner_thought: I checked the scheduled pipeline on the ML platform, and from my perspective the benchmark is the registered job that productionized Nina's work, including the platform defaults. I need to keep this from turning into 'the migration broke it' unless we can actually trace a concrete issue. Reproducibility means the same commit and registered assets should regenerate the same fold outputs and artifacts, not just roughly similar top-line metrics.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I pulled the logs from the scheduled run this morning. I agree we need to get reproducibility back before this goes any wider. Right now I can see the job completed cleanly, but that obviously doesn't help if the benchmark is moving around underneath us.

turns.inner_thought: The model code hasn't changed in the official comparison config, and with the same seeds and package versions inside the training container, these tabular models should not swing that much. Hardware or launcher differences shouldn't matter here. So my first instinct is still that something drifted in what I'd call the same environment, maybe a dependency bump or parameter file mismatch.
turns.utterance: My first guess is that something drifted in the same environment, because the model code and seeds should be stable. A drop this large doesn't feel like random noise to me.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I'll diff the full execution envelope from the last known-good registered run: image digest, runner type, CPU arch, orchestrator defaults, mounted preprocessing module, the lot. If something changed in the platform context, I want a precise line item so infra doesn't get blamed vaguely.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can diff the same environment against the last successful run we have on record, including the runner settings and any attached preprocessing components, and see if anything shifted between the two executions.

turns.inner_thought: It's notable that the anomaly is concentrated on Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4, which in my mind means the cleaned snapshots for those datasets may have been handled differently somehow. If the issue were truly global, I'd expect broader movement across the benchmark table.
turns.utterance: What stands out to me is that this seems pretty isolated to Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4. That makes me wonder whether one of those datasets got handled differently in the rerun.

turns.inner_thought: I should verify the dataset asset IDs behind Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4. Those names are stable in the registry, but the underlying assets may have refreshed from raw ingests without changing the human-readable label. If the scheduled job pulled the latest registered copies, that could fully explain a metric shift without any code change.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's worth checking. I'll verify the asset versions for Eclipse-3.0 and Lucene-2.4 and confirm whether the platform pulled the latest registered copies during the scheduled job.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get the benchmark table back into the prior AUC and recall range, then I can reasonably frame this as a reproducibility hiccup rather than a substantive flaw in the modeling setup. I really need the published comparison configuration to remain defensible.
turns.utterance: From my side, if we can restore the benchmark table to roughly the prior range, that's probably enough to treat this as a reproducibility hiccup rather than a modeling problem. I mostly want to make sure the comparison we're referencing still holds up.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want us to call it fixed just because the summary table looks familiar again. For me, reproducibility is back only when the same commit and pinned assets produce matching fold-level outputs and tracked artifacts. Otherwise we're papering over a lineage problem.
turns.utterance: I hear you. For me, the key checkpoint is that we can rerun the same commit and get matching fold artifacts back from the tracker. Once that lines up again, we'll know reproducibility is fixed.

turns.inner_thought: Fastest path on my side is to compare the earlier comparison config and the package lock from the benchmark notebook setup. If those are unchanged, that strengthens my view that the core pipeline is fine and this is a local reproducibility issue rather than a benchmark design problem.
turns.utterance: As a quick pass, I can compare the current run against the earlier benchmark configuration file and the package lock. That should tell us pretty quickly what changed, if anything obvious did.

turns.inner_thought: I also need to inspect whether the platform's default tabular preprocessing module was attached in the scheduled pipeline and whether a dataset registry refresh altered effective inputs while keeping the visible names the same. That's exactly the kind of silent difference people miss when they assume the scheduled job is identical to the original benchmark.
turns.utterance: Good. In parallel, I'll inspect whether the default tabular preprocessing step or a dataset registry refresh changed the effective inputs without changing the visible job name. Those are the kinds of things that can make two runs look equivalent when they aren't.

turns.inner_thought: I'll rerun XGBoost locally on the cleaned Eclipse-3.0 parquet snapshot from last month, using the same package versions and seeds as the official benchmark setup. If recall looks normal there, then the issue is unlikely to be the modeling setup itself. I don't think hardware or orchestrator details should matter for this kind of tabular pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: I'll pin the dataset asset IDs and capture the full environment digest from the scheduled run so we have a proper reproducible baseline in the platform sense. Then we can see whether the issue is lineage, infra context, or something upstream. I want a concrete audit trail before anyone says the benchmark is stable again.
